report:
**Conclusion: Yes.** Heavy current and former smokers are significantly less likely to die of lung cancer if they participate in regular screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT).

### Key Evidence

1. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST):** This landmark U.S. randomized controlled trial involving over 53,000 high-risk individuals demonstrated a **20% reduction in lung cancer mortality** among participants screened annually with LDCT compared to standard chest X-rays. (Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873)

2. **NELSON Trial:** A major Dutch-Belgian randomized trial evaluating over 15,000 high-risk individuals confirmed these results. At 10 years of follow-up, volume-based LDCT screening led to a **24% reduction in lung cancer mortality** in men (and 33% in women) compared to no screening. (Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793)

3. **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF):** Based on trial evidence, the USPSTF recommends annual LDCT screening for adults aged 50–80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. (Source: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2777242)

### How It Works
Screening does not prevent lung cancer itself, but LDCT scans detect nodules early—at localized stages (Stage I/II)—when surgical resection and curative treatments are far more effective, preventing progression to lethal, advanced-stage disease.
